7ater is one of the most essential 
Wrequirements of life. Assured availability of 
potable water is vital for human 
development. India is home to 18% of global human 
population and 15% of global livestock population. 
However, it has only 2% land mass and 4% of global 
freshwater resources. As per estimates²; in 1951, per 
capita annual freshwater availability was 5,177 cubic 
meters which came down to 1,545 cubic meters in 
2011. It is estimated that in 2019, it is about 1,368 cubic 
meters which is likely to further go down to 1,293 cubic 
meters in 2025. If present trend continues, in 2050, 
freshwater availability is likely to decline to 1,140 cubic 
meters. 
With the growing population and expanding economic 
activities, there is an increase in demand for water in 
various  sectors, viz. agricultur e, indus try, domes tic, 
recreation, infrastructure development, etc., whereas 
the source of water is finite. Thus, finite availability and 
competing demands make drinking water management 
a complex issue. The widening demand-supply gap is 
further compounded by other challenges, viz. depletion 
of groundwater caused by over-extraction, poor 
recharge, low storage capacity, erratic rainfall due to 
climate change, presence of contaminants, poor 
Operation and Maintenance (O&M) of water supply 
systems, etc.
In pre-Independent India, the wate r management 
systems and structur es were adequa te to cater to the 
low popula tion. Local communities have been known 
for designing their own systems using traditional 
knowledge and wisdom to fulfill needs of the 
community in different edapho-clima tic conditions. 
How ever, with increasing popula tion and disruption in 
rainfall pattern and decr ease in storage, challeng es 
related to scarcity of water have become acut e.
Post Independence, the State Governments have 
implemented rural water supply programmes to 
provide safe drinking water to rural population. In 1972, 
as part of Minimum Needs Programme, Government of 
India started supporting States through Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP). Since then, 
Government of India has taken a number of initiatives 
to assist the States in their endeavor to enable every 
rural household to have access to potable water.Under the erstwhile National Rural Drinking Water 
Programme (NRD WP), 2017, one of the objectiv es was 
to 'enable all households to have access to and use safe 
& adequa te drinking water within premises to the 
extent possible' which was proposed to be achie ved by 
2030, coinciding with the Unit ed Nation's Sustainable 
Developmen t Goals (UN-SDG 6).  
Piped water supply for drinking and domes tic purposes 
to rural areas is a very critic al and challenging task. 
Over the years, some import ant lessons have been 
learn t from the water supply programmes, which inter-
alia include:
i.) inadequate investments to meet both capital 
requir emen ts as well as Oper ation & Main tenance 
(O&M) led to incomple te and/ or defunct water 
supply systems;
ii.) mos t of the rural water supply schemes being 
dependan t on ground water, withdr awal of excess 
ground wate r for agricultural purposes led to 
systems not serving the full design period;
iii.) sour ce sustainability measur es such as aquif er 
rechar ge, rain water harvesting, increased storage 
capacity of water bodies, reser voirs, de-silting , etc. 
impr ove the lifespan of water supply systems;
iv.) quite often, poor main tenance of schemes led to 
investmen ts going waste;
v.) there is a willingness by community to pay for 
water, provided there is an assured service

8.7  Water audit and water security
With water availability becoming scarce due to 
multiple reasons, time has come to enforce audit of 
water supplied regularly to reduce the losses in the 
distribution system. Ther e are two types of losses, real 
and appar ent losses. Real loss includes water lost 
through leakages in distribution systems, service 
connections and storage tanks (including overflow). 
Appar ent loss includes meter and record inaccur acies 
and unauthorized water uses such as theft and 
unauthoriz ed connections. In order to impr ove the 
efficiency of the water supply systems, States are to 
regularly take up water audit of iden tified systems for 
effectiv e impr ovemen t.
In order to ensur e that the investmen ts made under 
the Jal Jeevan Mission lasts on long-t erm basis, it is 
import ant to prepar e the water budg et of the villag e by 
assessing the total available water from all sour ces 
(both ground and surface). Further , water use for domes tic/ agricultur e/ indus trial purposes, etc. have to 
be assessed. 
Overdraw of and its inefficien t use in agricultur e leads 
to depletion of ground/ surface wate r sources in 
villag es, seriously affecting the drinking water security . 
The w ater budg et prepar ed as part of the V AP is t o be 
dissemina ted among the local community so that they 
can be sensitiz ed to impr ove the agricultur e water-use 
efficiency by adopting micr o-irrig ation and/ or adopt 
cropping pattern suiting the agro-clima tic zone. In 
addition to the abov e, using funds available under 
various schemes like MGNREGS, State schemes, 
PMK SY, etc., scien tific rechar ge of deple ted ground 
water aquif ers in the villag e can be done, thereby 
enhancing ground water levels and ensuring water 
security for drinking during summer mon ths.
Man y States have already taken up such conser vation 
measures and have improved the groundwater 
availability . The recen tly concluded Jal Shak ti Abhiy an, 
an intensiv e campaign for conser vation of water, has 
gener ated awareness among the public and farmer s on 
water conser vation and impr oved agricultur e water 
use efficiency . States can take up such campaigns 
under IEC activities for long-t erm water security .   Technological Inter ventions and Inno vations

92.1   Historical perspectiv e  
Post-independence at the time of launch of India's 
planned development, the Environmental Hygiene 
Commit tee recommended a programme to provide 
safe water supply to all villag es within a certain period 
as part of First Five Year Plan (1951-56). For this 
purpose, the National Water Supply Programme was 
launched in 1954, under the health sector. 
Until the Third Five Year Plan (1961-66), drinking water 
suppl y in the rural areas was a compone nt of the 
Communi ty Developme nt Programme . This effort was 
suppl emented by the Ministry of Health unde r the then 
National Water Suppl y and Sanitation Programme . 
In 1972-73, Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP) was launched to supplemen t the 
efforts of State Governmen ts, especially in areas of 
acute scarcity and those endemic to water borne 
diseases. The programme gained further momen tum 
during the Fifth Five Year Plan (1974-79) under the 
Minimum Needs Programme. 
In 1986, the National Drinking Water Mission (NDWM), 
popularly known as the Technology Mission was 
launched in order to provide scien tific input and cost-
effective technological solutions to address wate r 
scarcity. 
In the Eigh th Plan (1992-97), Sub-missions for tackling 
quality pr oblem, i.e. habit ations suf fering fr om e xcess 
Arsenic, Fluoride, Iron, salinity, scarcity of water

the systems, were taken up. 
In 1999-2000, decentralized, demand-driven, 
community -manag ed sector reforms  were undert aken 
involving Gram Panchayats/ local community in 
planning, implementation and management of 
drinking water schemes. This was later scaled up as 
Swajaldhar a in 2002 and was implemen ted till 2007-08.  
In 2004-05, ARWSP became part of Bhar at Nirman 
aiming a t full c overage of habit ations by 2008-09. The 
ARWSP was implemen ted till the year 2008-09 of 
Eleventh Plan (2007-12). In 2009-10, it was modified 
and renamed as National Rural Drinking Water 
Programme (NRDWP) with major emphasis on ensuring sustainability of water availability in terms of 
potability , adequacy , convenience, affordability and 
equity , on a sustainable basis, adopting decen tralized 
appr oach involving Pancha yati Raj Institutions (PRIs) 
and community organizations. 
In 2013, certain chang es were introduced in NRD WP, 
viz. i.) providing focus on pipe water supply schemes;

quality and Japanese Encephalitis-Acut e Encephalitis

In 2017, NRD WP was restructur ed to i.) mak e it more

The decline in water availability and its quality

industrial and agricultural activities and climate 
chang e driven alterations to the hydrologic al cycle has 
become a global phenomenon. The monit oring and 
surveillance of water quality is now imper ative.
It is important to note that, the community accords 
great priority for access to water, but water quality 
issues do not attract similar attention. This is because, 
at grassroots, water quality is usually ascertained only 
by color, odour and taste of the water. The presence of 
most of the chemical contaminants does not exhibit any 
change in terms of color, odour or taste in comparison 
with potable water and the communities continue to 
consume the quality-affected water in ignorance of 
potential threats of consuming  such  contamina ted

to use quality-affected water for cooking purposes.

and education on water quality and engage

Water is a basic necessity. Lack of assured availability of potable water adversely impacts households and local 
communies. In the absence of access to potable drinking water at home, families, especially women and young girls 
are forced to spend lots of me and energy every day in carrying water to their homes. During scarcity, State 
Governments/ local administraons take emergency measures to provide water through tankers, trains, etc. With the 
Government taking a number of steps to improve 'ease  of  living', people now expect tap water supply in their homes.
In this back drop, Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM)  has been launched in partner ship with States, to enable every 
household in villag es to have Funconal Household Tap Connecon (FHT C) in the next 5 years. It is envisag ed that 
with FHTC, each household will have potable water supply in adequa te quan ty of prescribed quality on regular 
and long-t erm basis. To implemen t the mission, instuonal arrangemen ts at various levels have  been made and 
State's PHE/ RWS Departmen ts are to play a cric al role. They have to help Gram Pancha yat and/ or its sub-
commi ee to plan, implemen t, manag e, oper ate  and main tain  its in-villag e  water  supply systems. A sense of 
owner ship has to be inslled in the villag e community as they are at the centre of this mission.
In villag es, local communies especially women, mus t be encouraged to parcipa te and take owner ship of water 
resour ce manag emen t, water supply , and greywater treatmen t and its reuse. To achie ve this, wher ever requir ed, 
in addion to PHE/ RWS departmen ts, Gram Pancha yats are to be assis ted by SHGs/ VOs/ CBOs/ NGOs, youth 
groups, etc. and ﬁnancial convergence with funding sour ces likes MGNRE GS, SBM, MPLAD , MLALAD , DMDF , 
dona ons, CSR funds, etc. to be made. To mak e water everyone's business, the mission will strive to build 
partner ships with developmen t  partner s, academic & technic al instuons  and work together to achie ve long-
term drinking water security .
Wher ever potable water is not available in adequa te quan ty, PHE/ RWS Departmen ts have to plan water transfer, 
its treatmen t and distribuon system. While planning water supply system, oper aon and main tenance is the 
mos t cric al aspect. It is import ant that water supply schemes funcon throughout their comple te design period. 
To ensur e that public investmen ts do not go to waste, there is a need to strengthen water sour ces especially in 
water-stressed areas. In water quality -aﬀected villag es, technologic al innov aons have to be explor ed. PHE/ RWS 
Departmen ts have to prepar e District and Villag e Acon Plans with the acv e parcipa on of villag e community . 
Following the 'bo om up appr oach', States are to prepar e Annual Acon Plan as well as ﬁve-year 'State Acon 
Plan' with deliv erables and melines, and implemen t the programme in mission-mode.
On behalf of the Departmen t, I would like to express our sincer e gratude to Hon'ble Prime Minis ter for providing 
the vision and impe tus to this mission. I sincer ely belie ve that this Oper aonal Guidelines  documen t will be 
immensely use ful in implemen ng the Jal Jee van Mission t o provide FHT Cs to every household and in achie ving 
long-t erm water security in every villag e.

6.1.4  Oper ation & Main tenance (O&M)
Oper ation & main tenance is import ant for ensuring

breakdown maintenance, remuneration of pump

6.2  R egional w ater supply and dis tribution 
network
In villages with water quality issues and paucity of 
surface water sources, especially in drought-prone and 
desert areas, to achieve water security bulk water 
transfer from long distances is a reality. Further, in 
drought-prone and desert areas, where it is not possible 
to have water supply through conjunctive use, a similar 
approach to transfer bulk water from long distance will 
be adopted. In States with water-scarce/ areas lying in 
rainshadow region with inadequate rainfall, it is 
necessary to plan for regional water supply schemes 
covering both urban and rural areas of this region by 
sourcing water from a perennial surface source. 
Since the water is transferred from long distance at a 
very high cost, it is essen tial to have least loss of water 
during transmission. For this purpose it is necessary to 
have District Metering Area (DMA) with SCADA 
systems and/ or sensor -based mechanism to reduce 
non-r evenue water.

Emer gency prepar edness for response
Prepar edness at all levels, i.e. Departmen tal (State 
level), district and villag e level is of utmos t import ance. 
Key elemen ts of prepar edness are:
I.) identification and access to trained human 
resour ces for post disas ter damag e & needs; 
ii.) assessment and planning for providing 
transitional services and; restoration of disas ter 
impacted systems. A sound and integrated 
training in related sectoral courses should be 
impart ed by the state governmen t; 
iii.) prepositioned emer gency water supply kits to 
provide transitional services in camps and other 
mass displacemen t situa tions; 
iv.) water quality surveillance with reference to 
disease surveillance as part of concurrent 
monit oring;
v.) adapt or design new systems to minimiz e local 
flooding , sewage overflow routing or storage; 
and 
vi.) build in preventive main tenance to clear drains 
and sewers regularly .
During disas ter: During this period, the needs and 
provisions of affected people are met to alleviate and 
minimiz e suffering. 
Key elemen ts of response to disas ter will be:
I.) access to trained & skilled human resour ces for 
providing transitional services;
ii.) access to prepositioned emer gency water supply 
kits camps and other mass displacement 
situa tions;iii.) setting up of mobile water purific ation plan ts in 
affected area;
iv.) water quality surveillance with reference to 
disease surveillance using field test kits;
v.) supply of adequa te purific ation kits.
Post-disaster: Providing potable drinking water and 
sanitation facilities during and post disaster situations 
like flood, cyclone, earthquake, etc. is one of the biggest 
issues and should be treated as a top priority. After a 
disaster, the key challenge is to achieve rapid and 
durable recovery which does not reproduce the original 
vulnerable conditions. Post disaster reconstruction aim 
is to restore pre-disaster water supply condition. This 
includes activities such as quick and effective 
replacement of damaged water source and water 
supply infrastructure. While doing so, due care needs to 
be taken for long-term development prospects and 
potential disaster proneness and ensure 'build back 
better' the water supply infrastructure. Thus, a 
conscious integration of disaster resilience into the 
material selection as well as construction planning will 
be done for disas ter proofing of the water suppl y 
infrastructure rather than reproducing the same 
conditions as were before.

For man y years, the Governmen t of India and State Governmen ts have been making eﬀorts to increase access to 
safe and adequa te drinking water to people.  At the top of the aspir aonal ladder has been household piped water 
supply , and yet only about 20% of rural households have access to tap water in their homes.  On Independence Day 
this year, from the Ramparts of the Red Fort, the Hon'ble Prime Minis ter made an iconic announcemen t - the 
Governmen t of India’ s resolv e to provide piped water supply for all households of India by 2024 under the Jal 
Jeevan Mission (JJM).
The JJM will aim to provide a Funconal Household Tap Connecon (FHT C) to every rural household in the country. 
It will promot e the manag emen t of water at the lowest appr opria te level through decen tralized, but integrated 
water resour ce management by the Gram Pancha yats, with a key focus on water conser vaon, sour ce 
sustainability , and rainwater storage. The JJM will also focus on developing infrastructur e for collecon and basic 
treatmen t of domes c non- fecal wastewater, also called greywater, which typic ally accounts for nearly 80% of all 
domes c water.
In groundw ater rich areas, single villag e groundw ater-based schemes with end to end sour ce sustainability 
measur es will be encouraged. In places wher e groundw ater is not abundan t, especially in the designa ted dark 
block s and in areas aﬀected by water quality issues, surface water based mul- villag e schemes will be promot ed.
Under the Prime Minis ter’s leader ship, the Jal Jeevan Mission will aempt to become a Jan Aandolan, just like the

8.3.1  Cold deserts
Cold deserts are primarily located in high altitudes in 
Himalayan region of Arunachal Pradesh, Ladakh, 
Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, etc. The primary 
sour ce of w ater in these ar eas is Glacial melt, which is 
being impact ed because of clima te chang e. Further , 
the water gets frozen in the pipelines during winters 
disrupting the water supply . Solutions may be explor ed 
to enhance and store run-of f water in small tanks - 
traditional water harvesting structure, i.e. zing. 
Further , artificial glacial reser voirs may be created by 
diverting the run-of f to freeze & store as glacier . During 
early spring , it will serve as both drinking water and 
irrigation sour ce. Promoting use of micr o-irrig ation can 
reduce the irrigation requir emen t and increase the 
drinking water security . 
8.3.2  Hard rock areas
In hard rock areas, Bore-blas t technique, fractur e seal 
cemen tation, stream blasting, etc. may be explor ed 
under skilled super vision for accessing groundw ater.
8.3.3  Hilly areas
In hilly areas, especially at higher altitudes, it is 
unec onomic al to pump water from the valley for a very 
small number of houses. In these places, adopting 
spring-based sour ces, rain water harvesting and stand-
alone bore-well systems (if feasible) will be 
economical. Spring based systems would require 
careful iden tification and delinea tion of spring-sheds, 
locating the aquif ers contributing water to springs and 
injection rechar ging them for sustaining them.
Communities may be encouraged to adopt the 
traditional wisdom of rain water harvesting (like 
bamboo based ones in NE States) for water security . In 
such areas, there is a need to focus on WQM&S.   
8.3.4  Coas tal areas 
In coastal areas, augmen tation of services can be done 
with ener gy efficien t small desalina tion plan ts with 
high recovery ratio. Further , in order to avoid the 
ingress of sea water, sub-surface dykes can be 
constructed in rivers that can also improve the groundwate r based drinking wate r sources in the 
adjoining areas. Funds under MGNREGS, State 
schemes can be utiliz ed for this purpose.

11.1  Monit oring
Effective monitoring mechanisms will ensure 
functionality of tap connections, i.e. drinking water 
supply in adequa te quan tity of prescribed quality on 
regular basis.   
JJM monitoring mechanisms comply with the global 
standards, viz. Global Competitiveness Index (GCI). GCI 
measures national competitiveness defined as 'set of 
institutions, policies and factors that determine the level 
of productivity'. GCI includes following two indicators:
i.) exposure to unsafe drinking water: It measures a 
population's exposure to unsafe drinking water, 
taking into account the extent of exposure by risk 
level and the severity of that risk's contribution to 
disease burden;
ii.) reliability of water supply: This is based on how 
reliable is the water supply (lack interruptions 
and flow fluctua tions).

monit oring

order to manag e both  the in-villag e infrastructur e

stand post, it is necessar y to have data on water 
suppl ied every day, the qual ity of water suppl ied as well

Prevention and Mitig ation
I.) improvement in water storage capacity of 
aquif ers is the best long-t erm strategy. Passiv e 
rechar ge of aquif ers particularly in forested areas 
is the mos t effectiv e water conser vation method 
for futur e drinking water security . Forests can 
hold lar ger volume of w ater for long er dur ations 
on the forest floor that acts like a spong e to slowly 
release water into streams; an example of how 
certain ec osystems ensur e water availability and 
flood risk reduction. How ever, this involves long-
term planning and action;
ii.) efforts towards increasing availability of quality -
water from shallow and deep aquif ers will ensur e 
water availability during periods of drough t and 
dela yed monsoon;iii.) presence of resilien t infrastructur e is rewarding

prone areas. Also , anchoring of pipes has to be

and chang e manag emen t
A public utility is an undert aking that provides essen tial 
services. JJM envisages a mindset change in the provision of drinking water supply services. The service 
provision should change from 'infrastructure 
developmen t appr oach' to a 'utility based appr oach'. 
For this, it is requir ed to re-orien t both engineering and 
other human resour ces. This would be undert aken

such service provision. The personnel managing the 
water supply services at all levels, i.e. villag e, GP, 
district and State, need to be provided with customiz ed 
training and leader ship programmes so as to enable 
them to dischar ge their role in managing these utilities. 
Chang e manag emen t is 'a structur ed appr oach for 
ensuring that chang es are thor oughly and smoothly 
implemen ted and that the lasting bene fits of chang e 
are achie ved'. It is the process of ensuring that an 
organisa tion institut es and supports beha viour s and 
tools that are necessary to achie ve short and long-t erm 
goals more efficien tly.
As part of these objectiv es, customised annual training 
calendar to be framed for engineering and manag erial 
cadre of the PHED/ RWS Departmen ts in States. The 
programme should be customiz ed to suit different 
levels covering various technical, managerial and 
leader ship aspects. It would compulsorily to have a 
two-week training and exposur e visit to countries that 
have excelled in rural water supply provision and the 
Departmen t/ National Mission would iden tify suitable 
partner s/ institutions both within the country and 
abroad. For long-term water security, concerted 
efforts need to be made to bring the mindse t chang e to 
mak e engineer s as Public Health Engineer s and Utility/ 
Service manag ers.

the positively tested samples referred by the sub-
division/ block laboratory/ mobile laboratory on at 
least for 13 basic water quality parameters. The

samples to the State laboratory immediately. The 
othe r parameters may be tested as per local 
contamination at district level. 
iii.) State laboratory: The State lab will test at least 5% 
of the total drinking water samples across all 
district level laboratories with random and 
uniform geographical spread including positively 
tested samples referred by district/ sub-division/ 
block/ mobile lab.  If the number of districts in any State/ UT is large (>50), then the testing of 
samples/ sources may be restricted to 3% for the 
State lab. Remaining 2% may be integrated with

Detailed Sustainability Matrix

Drinking Water Sustainability Matrix:

i. Institutional and Service Delivery Sustainability: The institutional framework and governance mechanisms
that enable water supply systems to operate professionally, accountably and sustainably, while delivering

assured service standards to all households:

a) Institutionalise accountability at all levels: State, District, PRI, VWSC/ GP and operators;

b) Assure service delivery and standards.

ii. Source Sustainability: The long-term security of water sources through groundwater recharge, source
protection and integrated water resource management ensuring adequate water availability year-round:

a) Secure water sources through hydrogeology-based planning, recharge structures, water quality surveillance
and infrastructure protection mechanisms.

iii. Financial Sustainability: The ability of water supply schemes to generate sufficient revenue through service
delivery charges to cover operational costs and maintenance, without perpetual subsidy dependence:

a) Ensure financial sustainability by instituting transparent tariff structures and strengthening revenue
collection mechanisms, while effectively communicating the intrinsic value of water services to end-users.

iv. Infrastructure Sustainability: Systematic management of water supply infrastructure assets through digital
registries, preventive maintenance scheduling, lifecycle costing and performance tracking ensuring long asset
life and operational efficiency:

a) Strengthen long-term asset management through asset and inventory management registry, O&M,
preventive maintenance and lifecycle costing.

Support Ecosystem of Sustainability Matrix:

i. Digital Systems: States to progressively adopt integrated digital systems to strengthen planning, monitoring
and accountability of rural water services. Development of GIS based asset registries, service area identifiers,
dashboards and decision support tools can enhance asset visibility, support informed decision making,
improve water quality surveillance and enable transparent service delivery across alllevels;

ii. Governance: States to strengthen governance structures by clarifying institutional roles, enhancing coordina-
tion across departments and aligning water policies with sustainability principles. Empowerment of local
institutions, promotion of regulatory mechanisms for source protection and standardization of asset manage-
ment and O&M practices can support resilient service delivery and longterm drinking water security;

iii. Community Ownership: States to encourage greater community ownership by enabling Gram Panchayats,
village institutions and local youth to participate actively in the management of rural water supply systems.
Structured capacity building programmes, clear operating procedures, local stewardship of water sources and
community engagement initiatives can foster asset ownership and sustainable operations;

iv. Citizen Feedback: States to strengthen citizen centric service assurance by institutionalizing feedback and
grievance redress mechanisms. Regular functionality assessments, transparent tariff communication, service
performance ratings, supply information systems and structured commissioning and handover processes can
improve responsiveness, build trust and support continuous service improvement.

Astrong nation is built on the well-being of its people and access to safe and clean drinking water remains central to
this goal. Water has always been an integral part of India's civilisation, shaping our lives, livelihoods and traditions,
where itis respected, conserved and celebrated.
However, for many years, ensuring reliable access to safe drinking water remained a challenge in rural India, especially
for women who bore the burden of fetching water.
The launch of the Jal Jeevan Mission marked an important step in addressing this challenge. In a short span, the
Mission has made significant progress, reaching the majority of rural households and improving quality of life through
the collective efforts of States, local institutions and communities. Its impact is visible across rural India, reducing
drudgery, improving health and nutrition and strengthening community ownership.
As we move into the next phase, the focus is on sustaining these gains. Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 marks a shift from
infrastructure creation to reliable service delivery, with Gram Panchayats and communities atthe centre.
Initiatives such as Jal Arpan and Jal Utsav are deepening Jan Bhagidari by fostering community ownership, while
Sujalam Bharat reflects a vision of transparent, technology enabled and citizen-centric water governance.
The operational guidelines for Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 provide a clear framework to strengthen institutions, enhance
accountability and ensure long-term sustainability of rural water supply systems, supported by key structural reforms
for effective operation and maintenance.
This Guidelines will play an important role in realising water security as.a key pillar of inclusive development in India's
journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047. By ensuring universal access to safe drinking water, India is contributing to
Sustainable Development Goal 6 and demonstrating how people-led development, supported by a whole-of-
governmentand whole-of-society approach, can deliver lasting outcomes.
With this, | urge all stakeholders, States, Districts, Gram Panchayats and Citizens, to work together with a shared sense
of responsibility. Through Jan Bhagidari, we can ensure that every village not only has access to water, but also
sustains it for the future.

Safe and reliable drinking water is the foundation ofa healthy, dignified and prosperous society. Through the Jal Jeevan
Mission, India has undertaken one of the largest transformations in rural water supply, bringing tap water to crores of
households and significantly improving the lives of millions, especially women and girls.
As we move into Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0, we are entering a new era where access to potable drinking water for every rural
household is becoming a reality. This is not merely about infrastructure; it is about ensuring a healthy and dignified life
forevery citizen.
In this phase, the focus must firmly shift to reliability of service delivery and Jan Bhagidari through GPs/ VWSCs
participation. States/ UTs must accord the highest priority to adherence to technical standards and protocols for quality
assurance. There must be regular and rigorous monitoring of works at all levels, ensuring that systems are built to last
and perform efficiently overtime.
The District Water and Sanitation Mission (DWSM) will play a central role in ensuring effective implementation and
oversight. At the same time, State Governments must put in place strong mechanisms for supervision, verification and
compliance. There must be zero tolerance for any irregularities or deviations from prescribed quality standards, as the
safety and well-being of citizens depend onit.
The introduction of Jal Utsavand a mandatory 15-daytrial period before handing overin-village infrastructure under Jal
Arpan, reflects this commitment to accountability and performance. It ensures that systems are tested, meet service
standards and deliver reliable supply before being entrusted to communities.
This has further strengthened the approach of Jal Sanchay, Jan Bhagidari & Catch the Rain Campaign in promoting
water conservation efforts. States/ UTs have been advised to take ground water recharge measures including rainwater
harvesting, borewell recharge and reuse of grey water, in convergence with schemes such as MGNREGS/ VB-G RAM Gand
SBM. These efforts will help ensure long-term sustainability of drinking water sources and reliable availability of water
for tap connections under the Mission.
At the same time, citizen accountability is at the heart of JJM 2.0. Through Jal Seva Aankalan, communities will play an
active role in assessing service delivery. These assessments will guide districts and States in preparing targeted service
improvement plans, ensuring that feedback from the ground directly shapes policy and implementation. In this way,
JJM 2.0 lays the foundation for strengthened rural drinking water governance, built on transparency, participation and
continuous improvement. ‘ ;

MESSAGE

Water has been revered in ourscriptures as the very source of life. As ourscriptures say, 71-1 qanete4 SM Nag Sha - May
the divine waters bringus welfare and nourishment.
The Jal Jeevan Mission has already brought about a transformative change to crores of rural households by providing
access to safe and adequate drinking water through individual household tap connections. Beyond improving the
quality of life, it has also strengthened public health outcomes and empowered India's Nari Shakti by reducing the
drudgery of fetching water from faraway sources.
Now, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 builds upon this strong foundation and takes this work to the next level. It establishes a
robust institutional framework for drinking water governance, complemented by digital data governance for rural
water supply systems. This phase introduces key reforms to enhance transparency, strengthen institutions and
improveservice delivery, supported by a comprehensive capacity-building framework.
Inthe true spirit of grassroots democracy, Gram Panchayats lie at the centre of this approach, envisioned as the owners
and operators of village water supply systems. With the support of digital platforms such as ‘Sujal Gaon’, they will be
better equipped to monitor, manage and maintain these systems. These tools will help connect village-level operations
with the broader water supply ecosystem, ensuring accountability from source to household.
As India advances through the Amrit Kaal towards Viksit Bharat, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 represents a growth from
enabling access through infrastructure creation to reliable and sustainable service delivery. This reflects our steadfast
commitment to ensuring regular water supply, assured water quality, source sustainability and efficient system
management for every household.
With continued community participation and the collective commitment of all stakeholders, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 will
furtherstrengthen India's journey towards a water-secure future.

3.3.10. SNA-SPARSH Framework and

Payment Mechanism

The SNA-SPARSH system has been envisaged as an

integrated financial framework connecting the Public

Financial Management System (PFMS), State Inte-

grated Financial Management Information System

(IFMIS) and the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) e-Kuber

platform. The SNA-SPARSH payment mechanism

enables NJJM to ensure just-in-time payments, thereby

significantly reducing unspent balances to near zero

and enhancing financial prudence, efficiency and

transparency. Key Features of SNA-SPARSH Implemen-

tation are asunder:

i. Integration with JJM-IMIS for Scheme-wise
Monitoring: The SNA-SPARSH module of PFMS
shall be integrated with JJM-IMIS to enable
scheme-wise payments and facilitate real-time
monitoring and reporting of financial progress;

ii. Structured Banking Arrangements Based on

Funding Pattern: States/ UTs with different
funding patterns for coverage and Support &
WQM&S components shall maintain separate SLS
and RBI accounts. States/ UTs with uniform funding
patterns shall maintain a single SLS and RBI
account for both components. The department
shall operate a single RBI account for release of the
central share;

Sujalam Shakti Group

Community-based organisations engaged by VWSC including village level Self Help Groups (SHGs, PACs, etc.) for

supporting safe, reliable and sustainable rural water services shall be referred to as Sujalam Shakti Groups. This will

help align these groups with the objectives of the Jal Jeevan Mission and recognise them as field functionaries for the

Mission. States may issue operational guidelines for these groups. These will preferably be women led community

support system for long-term functionality and sustainability of rural water supply schemes. Under this convergence

framework, identified groups may be oriented and trained to undertake structured roles in coordination with Gram

Panchayats and VWSCs, including:

i. Apply Basic Concepts of Rural Water Supply;

ii. Take uprelevant WOM&S activities at village/ GP level, Conduct Drinking Water Quality Testing using Field Test Kit
(FTK) and Perform Basic Water Disinfection using Chlorine, Bleaching Powder, etc. including:

a. Water quality testing and reporting: Conduct periodic testing of drinking water sources and household supply
using FTKs.and reportresults on designated digital platforms fortimely action;

b. Remedial action support: Coordinate with VWSCs, Gram Panchayats and technical functionaries for prompt
remedial measures in case of contamination or service disruptions;

c. Community surveillance: Support village level vigilance on protection of drinking water sources and infrastruc-
ture from contamination, misuse or damage and promote safe water handling practices.

iii. Support utility tariff collection and community engagement:

a. Awareness and facilitation for service delivery charge: Undertake awareness and mobilisation for timely payment
of service delivery charge and responsible water use for sustainable O&M, IEC & BCC activities etc;

b. Collection of service delivery charge: Where authorised by the Gram Panchayat/VWSC, SHGs may support collec-
tion of service delivery charge and maintenance contributions in a transparent and accountable manner through
digital orreceipt-based systems.

iv. Use Digital, Financial, Communication Skills and Customer Service including grievance redressal at the
Workplace;

v. Implement Source Contamination Prevention and Follow Regional Water Safety Guidelines:

a. Source sustainability: Facilitate community mobilisation for water conservation, recharge and source protection
through convergence with VB-G RAM Gand other local programmes.

Skill Development and LocalO&M Support

The component may include structured skill development of Sujalam Shakti groups to support minor operation and

maintenance activities at the village level. Through appropriate training and resource support systems, selected SHG

members may be trained in:

i. Basic upkeep and cleaning of water supply infrastructure such as overhead tanks, pump houses and surround-
ings;

ii. Support forminor repair and preventive maintenance activities under supervision of VWSC/DTU;

iii, Record-keeping and reporting of functionality issues;

iv. Supportservices forvillage level water system management.

Cluster-based training platforms and resource augmentation mechanisms etc. may be utilised for periodic capacity

building, refresher training and creation of a pool of trained community resource persons. This will not only

strengthen sustainability of water supply systems but also create locallivelihood opportunities for SHG members.

The Jal Jeevan Mission has brought about a significant transformation in rural water supply by expanding access to tap
water across the country. As we move into the next phase, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 seeks to consolidate these gains by
focusing on sustainability, efficiency and accountable service delivery.
This phase places strong emphasis on institutional reforms to strengthen drinking water governance across all levels. A
clear institutional architecture has been outlined, defining roles and responsibilities from the National to the Gram
Panchayat level, with a particular focus on empowering local institutions for effective service delivery. The District Water
and Sanitation Mission (DWSM) and District Technical Units (DTUs) will play a critical role in ensuring technical robust-
ness and implementation oversight.
At the village level, the Gram Panchayat, through its standing committee for water and sanitation (VWS5C), is positioned
at the core of service delivery. The VWSC will function as the executive arm of the Gram Panchayat, responsible for day-
to-day management, monitoring and upkeep of water supply systems. Strengthening these standing committees is
central to ensuring ownership, accountability and sustainability of services at the grassroots level.
Akey element of these reforms is the deepening of community participation. Community-based organisations such as
Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) will play an active role in supporting O&M,
monitoring and local management overseen byVWSCs. This approach aims to build ownership, strengthen accountabil-
ity and ensure long-term sustainability of water supply systems.
The guidelines also emphasise digital governance and data-driven monitoring, with the use of interactive dashboards at
National, State, District and Panchayat levels. Integration with citizen interface platformssuch as Meri Panchayat Mobile
Application will enable real-time feedback, grievance redressal and participatory monitoring, thereby strengthening
transparency and responsiveness in service delivery.
These reforms also focus on strengthening technical standards, improving operational efficiency and ensuring
consistent service delivery outcomes. Together, all the measures aim to transition the sector from a scheme-based
infrastructure creation approach toa service-oriented, lifecycle-based regular water supply systems in rural india.
Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 represents a comprehensive effort to build resilient and sustainable rural water supply systems
through strong institutions, empowered communities and effective governance mechanisms. | am confident that these
guidelines will support States, UTs in achieving the Mission's objectives and ensuring reliable drinking water services for
every rurallhousehald.

Jal Jeevan Mission has significantly improved rural drinking water access by bringing tap water within household
premises. In JJM 2.0, the focus now shifts from creating infrastructure to ensuring reliable and sustained water service
delivery. The Cabinet has approved service-delivery orientation and the guidelines reflect that direction. The heart of
JJM 2.0 is strong digital governance through the Sujalam Bharat digital framework. Every village is being assigned a
Sujal Gaon ID, mapping the entire system from source to tap. This strengthens transparency, avoids duplication and
supports better monitoring. Interactive dashboards and near real-time information flow are ensuring early flagging of
problems and quick corrections, which is very important. Command and Support Centres to ensure that projects are
built correctly and function as per plan. JJM 2.0 calls for stronger implementation systems and structural reforms.
States/ UTs to prepare and follow Comprehensive Implementation and Reform Plans (CIRP) to document road maps
forscheme completion, handing overto GPs and actions needed to keep those working.
Technical compliance remains a key requirement. Following CPHEEO norms and ensuring precise validation, States/
UTs will help in maintaining the construction quality, fair use of funds and sustainability. Decision Support Systems
(DSS) will integrate groundwater status, scheme-level data and field observations to help DWSMs plan better and act
faster, ultimately to support improved functionality. Districts are to provide technical support to GPs through District
Technical Unit (DTU), monitor progress and guide O&M practices. The idea of district-level leadership was boosted
during the 700-plus interactions with District Collectors held over last one year. Those interactions shaped the struc-
tural reforms, especially the shift towards accountability and monitoring. Initiatives like Peyjal Samvad further
strengthened the message that DWSMs must develop practical solutions, improve preventive maintenance and adopt
cost-effective practices suited to local needs. Similarly, village-level conversations like Sujal Gaon Samvad helped
communities understand their roles in keeping systems functional and reporting service gaps. As JJM 2.0 places GPs at
the centre of service delivery, schemes will be handed over through Jal Arpan, after 15 days trial run and verification to
strengthen the O&M ecosystem through Jan Bhagidari. Villagers will come together in annual Jal Utsav, as a mark to
restore commitment towards drinking water.
JJM 2.0is a step toward a stronger, transparent, community owned and managed rural water service framework. As we
begin this phase, our goal is clear: to build a service oriented, accountable and community led water supply system.
The guidelines that follow reflect the structural reforms approved by the Cabinet and outline how States/ UTs, districts
and GPs can work together to achieve this. | am confident that with collective effort, close attention to technical
standards and steady implementation of CIRP, we will ensure that every rural household receives reliable drinking
